narration.text: This is Drizzle. He lives in Gull Harbor, Washington. Two thousand people, one road out, and one of the most dangerous fault lines in North America just off the coast.
Drizzle wasn't a prepper. But one fact had stuck with him. On this coast, if the ground shakes hard, the ocean can arrive in about fifteen minutes.
At 10:42 on a Tuesday, his coffee started to shiver. Then the floor moved.
His first instinct was the doorway. Most people's is. But in a modern house, a doorway is no stronger than the rest of the wall, and it's exactly where things fall.
So he did what the drills teach.
Drop before the quake drops you. Cover your head under something sturdy. Hold on to it, because the table will move, and you need to move with it.
Mags, his neighbor, was already under there. She'd come over for coffee. She'd done this drill every October for thirty years.
Ten seconds. Thirty. A minute. Small quakes end fast. This one kept going.
Four minutes of shaking. That told Drizzle everything. This was the big one. And the clock in his head started counting down.
Then the lights went out.
The shaking stopped at 10:46. If the ocean came in fifteen minutes, it would arrive around 11:01. The walk to high ground took twelve.
Three minutes. No time to pack a life. No time to look for keys or check the news.
He grabbed his laptop. His photo album. A plant. Then he put them all down.
The go-bag by the door was packed for exactly this. Water, a flashlight, a radio, medicine, a warm layer. One bag. Three seconds.
She was right. With the power out, the sirens might never sound. On this coast, the shaking is the warning.
Outside, the street had cracked open. And down at the harbor, the water was leaving.
Boats sat in the mud. A few people walked out to look. That's the deadliest mistake on the coast. When the sea pulls back, it comes back bigger.
Harbor Way was already jammed. One crack in the road can stop a thousand cars. It can't stop two people on foot.
So they walked. Uphill. Right now.
The evacuation route was point four miles of steep, muddy trail. Twelve minutes, on a good day.
Halfway up, an aftershock hit. No table out here. So they got low, covered their heads, and stayed clear of the trees.
Then Mags' knees gave out. Drizzle didn't argue. He gave her his shoulder, and they kept moving. Slower, but moving.
The official warning came twenty minutes after the shaking started. Anyone who waited for it was already out of time.
At the switchback, Drizzle looked back. A gray line stretched across the horizon.
At 11:04, the first wave hit Gull Harbor. It took the dock. The ferry. Then Main Street.
And the first wave is rarely the last. Tsunamis come in sets, for hours. You don't go back down until officials say it's safe.
The hilltop was cold, crowded, and above the water. Drizzle checked what he had.
Water first. One gallon per person, per day. His bag held three days.
Food second. About two thousand calories a day, for three days. That's the minimum. Out here, they tell you to plan for two weeks.
Drizzle counted what he'd done right.
One. Drop, cover, hold on. Two. On the coast, the shaking is your warning. Walk uphill, now. Three. Grab the go-bag, not your stuff.
And four. He'd packed snacks. Mags took one without a word.
Then the radio spoke again.
The only road out was gone. The whole coast had been hit at once, so help would come by air and sea, and it would take days.
Below them, the water was still rising. Night was coming. And somewhere down in the dark, a light flickered on where no one should be.
